title: Image-sensor floating-diffusion readout replaces bitline charge sharing
idea: First principles: a 5 fF cell at 0.5 V holds ~15,600 e-, yet CMOS image sensors resolve ~1 e- because they fully TRANSFER charge onto a ~0.5 fF floating diffusion instead of sharing it with a ~40 fF bitline. Build the DRAM cell as a pinned storage node + transfer gate into a floating diffusion shared by 4-8 cells, read by a local source follower (~300 uV/e-), so a ~500 e- (0.1 fF) cell gives a ~150 mV signal.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1): required Cs drops ~30x, so pillars no longer need AR 60-75:1 and 3D tiers get far easier; periphery SA offset budget relaxes.

title: Partial-charge sip read makes DRAM sensing non-destructive
idea: A tightly controlled subthreshold wordline pulse lets only ~3% of the cell charge (~450 e-) leak into a 0.2 fF local sense node; kT/C charge noise there is ~6 e-, so 450 e- is a >20 sigma signal (~0.36 V). The cell keeps 97% of its charge, so nothing is restored and only the addressed 64 B is sensed; normal refresh tops cells up.
why: Kills destructive read and 128x overfetch (fact 8): per-useful-bit read energy from ~5.9 pJ toward ~0.1-0.3 pJ; also removes row-activation hammer stress.

title: Coincident dual-gate matrix wordline addressing cuts drivers to 2sqrtN
idea: Decoding a row needs only log2(N) bits of information, yet DRAM spends one 3 V driver per row. Use a dual-gate access transistor whose front gate is a row-group line and back gate a sub-row line; it conducts only when both are high, so 1024 rows need 32+32 drivers instead of 1024 (display-style matrix addressing inside the mat).
why: Periphery area (fact 7): sub-wordline driver strips shrink ~10x, ~8-12% die area recovered; fewer high-voltage devices.

title: Breathing mat back-plate lowers wordline swing to 1.3 V
idea: The 3 V wordline exists only because Vt must be high for retention. Make Vt dynamic: a mat-shared back-gate plate sits at -1 V in standby (deep off, leakage tail suppressed) and steps to 0 V only for the accessed mat, so the wordline needs ~1.3 V and its drivers become thin-oxide core devices.
why: Voltage floor and periphery (facts 7, 10): wordline CV^2 energy ~5x lower ((3/1.3)^2), driver area ~3x smaller, charge pump eliminated or shrunk.

title: Column-parallel single-slope ramp sensing reads two bits per cell
idea: Borrow image-sensor column ADCs: one global ramp shared by 8k columns, a tiny comparator plus 3-bit counter per column digitizes the bitline twice (precharge and signal) and subtracts digitally (digital CDS). Offset and kT/C cancel in the subtraction, giving enough resolution to store 4 charge levels per cell.
why: Density/cost per bit: 2 bits/cell = ~2x bits per array area without litho shrink (fact 4); offset no longer sets the minimum signal.

title: Bitline segments become the successive-approximation capacitor DAC
idea: For multi-level read, split each bitline into binary-weighted segments (1:2:4 units of cells) with segment switches and perform charge-redistribution SAR using the bitline's own parasitic capacitance as the DAC; the parasitic that normally kills signal becomes the converter's reference.
why: Enables MLC DRAM sensing with ~zero added capacitor area; ~1.5-2x density at modest periphery cost (facts 1, 7).

title: Electrometer-style active guard bootstraps away bitline capacitance
idea: Parasitic capacitance only steals signal if its far plate moves differently from the bitline. Run a shield conductor between/under bitlines driven by a unity-gain bootstrap buffer that follows the bitline pair's common node (the electrometer guard trick), cutting effective Cbl ~5x.
why: Signal = Q/(Cs+Cbl_eff): ~4-5x more signal or ~4x smaller Cs at equal margin (fact 1); allows 2-4x longer bitlines, halving SA count (fact 7).

title: Varactor-state cell read by reactance without removing charge
idea: Store the bit on a MOS capacitor biased so '1' is accumulation (high C) and '0' depletion (low C); read with a small AC probe through the access device and measure the reactance in a bridge, which moves no net charge off the cell. Measuring a reactive parameter costs ~zero dissipated energy in the ideal limit.
why: Non-destructive read removes restore energy and page overfetch (fact 8); also lengthens effective retention because reads stop disturbing cells.

title: Geiger-mode avalanche sense node gives digital output from 100 electrons
idea: Bias a tiny junction just above breakdown with a quench resistor; a '1' cell injects hundreds of carriers that trigger avalanche with near-unity probability, a '0' injects none, so the sense node outputs a full-rail digital pulse with no linear amplifier. Dark-count false triggers are handled by a short gated window plus ECC.
why: Cs could fall ~100x (fact 1) and the SA collapses to a quench + latch; strong density and periphery-area gain if dark counts can be tamed.

title: Frequency-addressed MEMS resonators select mats over one wire
idea: Give each mat's enable a MEMS resonator relay with a unique resonant frequency on a shared bus; driving the bus at f_k rings up only resonator k and closes its mat switch, replacing a mat-select decoder tree with one address wire (orthogonal frequency channels as the address code).
why: Removes global decoder wiring and pre-decode buffers from the periphery (fact 7); suits slow mat power-up/select, not ns row access.

title: Zero-entropy token row selection for AI weight streaming memory
idea: AI inference reads weights in a fixed order, so the address entropy per access is ~0 bits; a full row decoder supplies log2(N) bits of random choice that are wasted. Replace decoders with a pitch-matched shift-register token that walks rows sequentially, keeping only coarse random access at mat level.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and energy: row decode area ~70-90% smaller in a streaming tier, plus predictable access removes most precharge/activate overhead.

title: Dumb-die DRAM moves DLL, training and refresh logic to controller
idea: Periphery logic on a DRAM process costs 3-4 logic generations more per transistor. Strip the DRAM die to array, sense and simple I/O; the controller on a leading logic node owns clock deskew (forwarded clock), PHY training, ECC, refresh scheduling and row-hammer tracking.
why: Periphery share of die (fact 7) falls by ~8-15 points; logic moves to where transistors are ~10x cheaper.

title: Controller-held repair map deletes on-die fuses and compare logic
idea: Repair information is only (#faulty rows x log2 N) bits, a few kbit, yet fuse banks and address comparators cost percent-level die area. Ship dies with no redundancy steering; the bad-row/column map measured at test is stored in the module SPD and the host controller remaps physical addresses.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): ~3-5% die area recovered; repairs become updatable in field.

title: Kerf-resident test periphery lives in scribe lanes
idea: Test-only circuits (BIST engines, test compression, probe pads) are used once but occupy die forever. Place them in the 60-100 um scribe lanes, wired to each die through traces that are severed at dicing, leaving only a minimal test port on the die.
why: Recovers ~2-4% of die area per wafer at zero process change (fact 7), more bits per wafer = lower cost per bit.

title: Stepwise adiabatic wordline charging with on-die tank capacitors
idea: Charging C through a switch to V always dissipates CV^2/2; charging in N equal steps from N-1 tank capacitors dissipates ~CV^2/(2N). Drive the 3 V wordlines and bitline restore in 4 steps from tank capacitors built in the array's own capacitor process.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): wordline/restore energy ~3-4x lower; charge-pump load and area drop too.

title: Self-decoding array builds decoders from vertical array transistors
idea: Instead of separate periphery CMOS, implement the row predecoder as a NAND-style ROM matrix made of the same vertical-channel transistors as the array, pitch-matched at array density and fabricated in the same steps.
why: Periphery area and process cost (facts 4, 7): decoder area ~3-5x smaller, fewer periphery masks.

title: Time-domain sensing via bitline-starved delay elements
idea: Convert the tiny bitline difference into a delay difference: the true and complement bitlines each set the current of a starved inverter chain, and a digital arbiter decides which edge arrives first, with a vernier for extra resolution. The SA becomes digital logic that scales with logic nodes.
why: Periphery area and voltage (facts 7, 10): SA shrinks and runs at core voltage; delay averaging over several stages reduces offset ~sqrt(N).

title: Negative-capacitance ferroelectric gate gives sense pair internal gain
idea: Add a thin HZO negative-capacitance layer in the gate stack of the sense amplifier's input pair so the internal channel potential swings more than the bitline (body factor < 1), amplifying a 50 mV signal ~2x before the latch fires.
why: Halves required cell signal or doubles tolerated Cbl (fact 1); longer bitlines cut SA count (fact 7).

title: BEOL oxide-TFT sub-wordline drivers stacked over the array
idea: Move sub-wordline driver strips out of silicon into a back-end thin-film transistor layer directly above the mats (wide-bandgap channel, high off-resistance suits 3 V switching), so the substrate under the array returns to cells or sense amps.
why: Periphery footprint (fact 7): ~10-15% die area freed without hybrid bonding.

title: Self-referenced double read only for test-flagged weak cells
idea: MRAM-style self-reference: read the cell, write a known '1', read again and compare both levels on the same SA input, cancelling per-cell Cs variation and SA offset. Applied only to the ~0.1% weak cells flagged at test via a small address table.
why: Lets the bulk population run with ~2x thinner margins (smaller Cs, longer refresh) while the tail is rescued (facts 1, 3).

title: Array-only fabs bond to US logic-foundry periphery wafers
idea: Split the business: a new entrant builds an array-only fab (capacitors and access devices, no periphery CMOS), and buys periphery wafers from US 22-28 nm logic foundries, joined by wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding with periphery under the array.
why: Capital intensity and US manufacturability (fact 4): array fab capex and mask count drop, periphery uses existing US capacity; ~30-40% lower entry capex.

title: Bucket-brigade CCD columns feed one floating diffusion per column
idea: For a streaming tier, arrange each 512-cell column as a charge-coupled shift register that clocks charge packets to a single floating-diffusion readout at the column end, as 1970s CCD memories did, but with modern 0.5 fF sense nodes reading ~1k e- packets.
why: Periphery collapses to one sense node per column, no per-bitline SA (fact 7); very high density for sequential workloads.

title: Margin-binned short-refresh SKU rescues dies failing JEDEC
idea: Dies that fail JEDEC sense margin at 85 C are binned (not scrapped) into a datacenter SKU whose controller runs 2x refresh and stronger ECC, with the measured margin written into SPD.
why: Raises usable supply by converting yield loss into product; few-percent more bits per wafer at zero capex.

title: BTI-balanced sense latches through epoch-wise data polarity swapping
idea: At 125 C, NBTI/PBTI shifts Vt ~10-30 mV over 10 years, mostly on whichever latch half sees one data value more often, eating a ~50 mV signal. Store every row inverted on alternate refresh epochs (one polarity bit per row) and swap which SA half is 'true', so both halves age equally to within ~1 mV.
why: Keeps sense margin intact for 10 y at 125 C without guardband; lets Cs stay ~20% smaller than an aging-guardbanded design (fact 1).

title: Idle-time sense-amp offset self-trim tracks aging in field
idea: Each SA gets a 4-bit current-injection trim; during refresh-idle windows it senses equalized bitlines (zero signal) and binary-searches the trim to null offset, re-running monthly so BTI drift at 125 C is continuously cancelled. Trim codes live in a reserved array row, not fuses.
why: Offset (~2,000 e- equivalent on 40 fF) is the real minimum-charge setter; nulling it lets Cs fall ~2x (fact 1) over the full 10-year life.

title: Leakage-replica analog refresh timer built from access transistors
idea: Make the refresh clock a capacitor discharged by a bank of access transistors identical to the array's (same doping, GIDL and junction), so its period follows the true leakage physics: ni ~7x up from 85 to 125 C and aging included, without temperature tables.
why: Refresh (fact 3): removes 2-4x worst-case guardband, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss at hot.

title: Ping-pong sense-enable drivers reverse current for electromigration healing
idea: Black's law makes Cu EM life ~19x shorter at 125 C than 85 C (Ea~0.9 eV), forcing wide SAN/SAP rails. Drive these rails from alternating ends on successive activations so current direction reverses, giving AC-like bidirectional stress with ~10x longer EM life.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): sense-enable and VARY straps can be ~2-3x narrower while meeting 10 y at 125 C.

title: Balanced-code words generate their own mid-level sense reference
idea: Encode each 64-bit word as a 68-bit constant-weight code (exactly 34 ones), so the average of the word's own bitlines is exactly halfway between its decayed '1' and '0' levels. A charge-sharing copy of the word's bitlines becomes the SA reference, tracking leakage at 125 C automatically.
why: Cells can decay much further before failure: ~2-4x longer refresh at hot for 6% bit overhead (fact 3).

title: Rank-modulation sensing via winner-take-all on charge order
idea: Store data as the ORDER of charge levels among a group of cells, read by a winner-take-all network that finds which cells hold the most charge. Uniform leakage at 125 C lowers all charges together but preserves order, so no absolute reference is needed.
why: Retention at hot (fact 3) decouples from absolute charge; refresh interval can stretch several-fold, and MLC-like density becomes possible.

title: FD-SOI periphery with PTAT back-bias flattens hot leakage
idea: Build periphery on fully-depleted SOI: buried oxide removes most junction area (generation leakage scales with ni and junction area), and a PTAT back-bias generator raises Vt ~1 mV/K as temperature climbs, holding standby leakage roughly flat from 25 to 125 C.
why: Periphery standby power at hot down ~5-10x; less self-heating feedback on retention.

title: Stacked thin-oxide cascode wordline drivers survive 125 C TDDB
idea: TDDB life shrinks exponentially with field and temperature, so 3 V drivers need thick, slow, large oxides. Split the swing across two series thin-oxide devices with a mid-rail cascode bias so each oxide sees ~1.5 V, inside its 10 y TDDB limit at 125 C.
why: Driver area ~2x smaller and faster than thick-oxide drivers (fact 7), with no lifetime penalty at hot.

title: Bipolar transistor sense amplifiers escape MOS mismatch and BTI
idea: BJT offset depends on emitter-area matching (sigma dVbe ~0.2-0.5 mV) rather than random channel dopants (MOS sigma Vt ~5-15 mV), and BJTs have no gate oxide to suffer BTI drift. Use vertical SiGe BJT latches in a BiCMOS periphery for sensing.
why: ~10x lower offset means ~5-10x less cell charge needed (fact 1); offset stays stable through 10 y at 125 C.

title: Automotive-grade MTJ storage holds trims and repair maps
idea: Floating-gate and charge-trap trims lose charge at 125 C, and e-fuses are one-shot. Store sense trims, timing codes and repair addresses in high-barrier MTJs (thermal stability Delta > 80, already qualified for 10 y at 150 C) beside the periphery, rewritable for in-field repair.
why: Enables in-field re-trim/repair at hot; replaces bulky fuse banks (fact 7) with ~10x denser nonvolatile bits.

title: Latch-resolution time flags convert errors into cheap erasures
idea: A weak (hot, leaky) cell produces a small signal and the latch resolves slowly; a timing comparator per SA group marks bits that resolved late as erasures. Reed-Solomon/BCH corrects 2 erasures for the cost of 1 error, so soft information is free.
why: ~2x stronger correction at the same parity, allowing ~2x longer refresh at 125 C or smaller Cs (facts 1, 3).

title: Access-is-refresh mapping puts hot pages on weak rows
idea: Every activation restores a row. The controller maps the most frequently accessed pages onto rows binned as weakest-retention at a 125 C test, so natural traffic refreshes them, while strong rows hold cold data with long refresh.
why: Refresh energy/bandwidth (fact 3) at hot cut ~30-60% with no hardware cost beyond a retention bin table.

title: Vt-tracking wordline high voltage relieves hot oxide stress
idea: Access Vt falls ~1 mV/K, so at 125 C the wordline needs ~100 mV less overdrive than at 25 C. Scale VPP down with temperature exactly by the Vt tempco, cutting oxide field when TDDB is most accelerated (~3x lifetime gain).
why: Enables thinner WL oxide and lower CV^2 energy at hot while meeting 10 y (fact 10).

title: Metal-contact NEMS relays power-gate mats and steer redundancy
idea: Mechanical relays have zero leakage and no oxide or junction to degrade at 125 C; their endurance limit (~1e10 cycles) is only a problem for fast paths. Use BEOL NEMS relays for mat power gating and redundancy steering, which switch only at boot or idle transitions.
why: Periphery standby leakage at hot -> ~0; relays sit above silicon, freeing area (fact 7).

title: Canary columns detect row hammer and hot retention together
idea: Reserve ~8 columns per row holding a known pattern written at a deliberately weaker level; whenever the row is opened (access or refresh) the SAs check the canaries for free. A flipped canary means the row's neighbors are hammered or leakage at 125 C is outrunning refresh, triggering targeted refresh.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) and retention (fact 3) monitored with ~0.1% area and no counters; physics-tracking at any temperature.

title: MIM-feedback charge amplifier sense with geometry-set gain
idea: Hold the bitline at virtual ground with a compact cascode integrator whose gain is Q/Cf, set by a MIM capacitor ratio rather than transistor Vt or mobility, so the output is independent of Cbl, temperature and aging.
why: Cbl no longer divides signal (fact 1): ~3-5x more output per electron, stable over 10 y at 125 C; longer bitlines cut SA count.

title: Zero-temperature-coefficient bias point fixes sense timing
idea: Mobility falls and Vt drops with temperature, and at one gate overdrive the two effects cancel (the ZTC point). Bias SA enable and timing replicas at ZTC so sense delay is flat from -40 to 125 C and timing guardbands can shrink.
why: tRCD/tRAS margins ~15-25% tighter, recovering bandwidth at hot (fact 3 bandwidth loss).

title: Plate-pulse charge boost during restore adds hot retention
idea: During restore, pulse the accessed mat's cell plate down by DeltaV, then release after the wordline closes: the storage node, now isolated, rises by ~DeltaV x Cs/(Cs+Cj), storing ~25% more charge without raising bitline voltage.
why: ~25% more charge = longer retention at 125 C or smaller Cs at equal retention (facts 1, 3).

title: Hot-mode dynamic twin-cell row pairing trades capacity for margin
idea: When a die or region runs hot, the controller pairs rows on complementary open bitlines into twin-cell mode (both wordlines fire, cells store opposite data), doubling differential signal and extending retention ~4-10x. Capacity halves only where and when needed.
why: Avoids designing all cells for worst-case 125 C retention (fact 1); refresh at hot drops sharply (fact 3).

title: Nano-vacuum-channel field-emission wordline drivers
idea: Electrons crossing a ~50 nm vacuum gap by field emission have no oxide to break down, no BTI, and no junction leakage; such switches tolerate far beyond 125 C. Use them as high-voltage wordline/plate switches fabricated in BEOL cavities.
why: Removes TDDB and BTI limits on 3 V drivers (fact 10) and moves drivers off silicon (fact 7).

title: AlN piezoelectric transformer replaces VPP charge pumps
idea: AlN is piezoelectric but not ferroelectric, so it cannot depolarize and works to >500 C. A thin-film AlN resonant piezo transformer steps 1.1 V up to 3 V at high efficiency, replacing multi-stage capacitive VPP/VBB charge pumps.
why: Periphery area and energy (facts 7, 10): pump area ~3-5% of die removed, conversion loss roughly halved.

title: Inductive coupling links replace TSVs in hot memory stacks
idea: At 125 C, Cu TSVs suffer protrusion and voiding under thermal cycling and add keep-out zones; inductive coil links (contactless, ~1 Gb/s per coil) carry data between stacked dies with no metal through silicon. Power still uses a few large TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): ~2x less area per bit, no TSV yield loss, reliable 10 y at hot.

title: US DRAM entrant leads with 125 C automotive and defense grade
idea: A new US memory maker first targets Grade-1 (125 C) automotive, industrial and defense DRAM, where self-calibrating periphery is a moat, volumes suit a modest fab and prices are high, then scales to datacenter.
why: US manufacturability and capital intensity: profitable at lower volume, builds the learning curve before competing on commodity cost.
